title: THE WOMEN WHO SPUN GOAT HAIR FOR GOD—AND THE FORGOTTEN TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR OWN LIFE
paragraphs: THE WOMEN WHO SPUN GOAT HAIR FOR GOD—AND THE FORGOTTEN TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR OWN LIFE

They weren't standing before crowds. They weren't performing miracles. Their names were never recorded. But their ordinary hands helped build a place where God's glory would dwell. And what happened in the wilderness may completely change how you see your hidden sacrifices, your painful past, and what you still have left to give Jesus.
There is something heartbreaking about giving everything you have and wondering whether anyone even notices.
You keep showing up.
You keep serving.
You keep praying when your heart is tired.
You keep giving when you have needs of your own.
And sometimes, when the room gets quiet, a question rises from somewhere deep inside you.
“Lord, does any of this actually matter?”
Maybe nobody sees what you do behind closed doors.
Maybe your family has no idea how much you sacrifice.
Maybe you've spent years believing that the only people who truly accomplish something for God are the ones standing behind pulpits, leading ministries, writing books, or speaking to thousands.
But buried in the book of Exodus is a remarkable account of women whose names we will never know.
They didn't preach a sermon.
They didn't command an army.
They didn't part the Red Sea.
They spun goat hair.
And God considered their work important enough to preserve it in Scripture.
Read that again.
The Creator of heaven and earth made sure future generations would know about women who worked with goat hair.
Not because goat hair was impressive.
But because what they did with it mattered.
And before this story is over, you may discover something about your own life that you've needed to hear for years.
Exodus 35:25–26 says:
“And all the women that were wise hearted did spin with their hands, and brought that which they had spun, both of blue, and of purple, and of scarlet, and of fine linen.
And all the women whose heart stirred them up in wisdom spun goats' hair.”
— Exodus 35:25–26, King James Version
At first glance, these verses might seem like a minor construction detail in a long description of Israel's wilderness sanctuary.
But there is something extraordinary happening here.
Something much bigger than fabric.
Something much deeper than craftsmanship.
And to understand it, we need to remember what happened before these women ever touched the fibers.
Because the story of the sanctuary begins in the shadow of a scandal.
Israel had witnessed the power of God.
They had seen the plagues fall upon Egypt.
They had walked through the sea on dry ground.
They had eaten bread from heaven.
They had heard the terrifying thunder of God's presence at Mount Sinai.
And yet, while Moses was on the mountain, the people turned their gold into an idol.
A golden calf.
They worshiped what their own hands had made.
They exchanged the glory of the living God for something that could neither hear their prayers nor save their souls.
Exodus 32 records the terrible betrayal.
And the consequences were devastating.
Sin had wounded the covenant relationship.
Judgment had fallen.
Moses had interceded.
The people had been confronted with the seriousness of their rebellion.
Then came one of the most astonishing developments in the entire story.
God had not abandoned His covenant purposes.
After the judgment and the renewal of the covenant, the people were called to participate in constructing the tabernacle according to the instructions God had given.
Think about the contrast.
Hands that belonged to a nation guilty of idolatry were now being invited to prepare materials for the worship of the true God.
The same people who had witnessed a catastrophic failure were being called into renewed obedience.
This was not because their sin had been insignificant.
It was because God's mercy had not disappeared.
And that is where this ancient story begins to reach into our own lives.
Because some of us know what it means to have a golden calf in our history.
Maybe yours wasn't made of metal.
Maybe it was pride.
Maybe it was money.
Maybe it was a relationship you placed above obedience to God.
Maybe it was an addiction you kept returning to.
Maybe it was the approval of people.
Maybe it was a secret compromise that slowly became more important than your devotion to Christ.
And now, whenever you think about serving God, your past whispers:
After what you've done?
After the promises you've broken?
After the prayers you've neglected?
After the times you've chosen yourself over Him?
You look at your hands and remember what they've done wrong.
But the Gospel announces something sin and shame cannot announce.
Jesus Christ came to redeem sinners, not to congratulate people who never needed mercy.
The tabernacle story does not teach that human effort can erase guilt. The sacrifices and priesthood of Israel pointed forward to the greater work that would be fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 9:11–12 presents Christ as the greater High Priest, who entered the holy place through His own blood, securing eternal redemption.
The Hebrew word מִשְׁכָּן (mishkan) means dwelling place or tabernacle.
The sanctuary was not simply a beautiful religious tent.
It was the appointed place associated with God's dwelling among His covenant people.
Exodus 25:8 records God's instruction:
“And let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them.”
Now consider this carefully.
The Lord who could not be contained by creation instructed His people to build a sanctuary where His presence would be manifested among them.
And part of that sanctuary would be prepared through the work of ordinary women.
Women whose names Scripture does not tell us.
Women whose family histories we do not know.
Women whose private struggles were never written down.
Women whose hands were skilled in work that many people today might consider unremarkable.
Yet their contribution became part of something sacred.
The Hebrew wording of Exodus 35:26 is especially beautiful.
וְכָל־הַנָּשִׁים אֲשֶׁר נָשָׂא לִבָּן אֹתָנָה בְּחָכְמָה טָווּ אֶת־הָעִזִּים
Ve-khol hannashim asher nasa libban otanah be-khokhmah tavu et-ha'izzim.
In context, this describes all the women whose hearts moved them in wisdom spinning the goat hair.
Notice the connection between the heart and the hands.
The text does not merely say that the women possessed a useful skill.
It tells us that their hearts moved them to use that skill.
The Hebrew word חָכְמָה (chokhmah) means wisdom, and in this context it includes the practical skill needed for craftsmanship.
Their wisdom was not merely theoretical.
It became action.
Their willingness did not remain a feeling.
It became work.
Their devotion was expressed through something they knew how to do.
And there is a lesson here that many believers desperately need to recover.
Not every act of worship looks like singing. Sometimes worship looks like faithfully doing the work God has placed before you.
Sometimes it looks like preparing a meal for someone who cannot repay you.
Sometimes it looks like caring for a sick parent.
Sometimes it looks like teaching a child to pray.
Sometimes it looks like working with integrity when dishonesty would be easier.
Sometimes it looks like serving quietly in a church where nobody knows how much effort your ministry requires.
And sometimes it looks like giving your time, abilities, or resources to help others encounter the truth of Scripture.
None of those actions automatically earns God's favor.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 makes clear.
But the very next verse says that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not purchase our obedience.
Grace produces a new reason to obey.
Now imagine the wilderness.
The tabernacle has not yet been completed.
There are no finished curtains enclosing its sacred spaces.
There is no completed structure standing in the camp.
There are materials to prepare.
There is work to be done.
Some people bring gold.
Others bring silver or bronze.
Some contribute precious stones.
Others offer wood, oil, spices, or fabric.
And among them are women spinning fibers.
It would be easy to assume that the most valuable gifts were the most impressive ones.
Gold catches the eye.
Precious stones attract attention.
But goat hair?
Coarse fibers worked into usable material?
Who would celebrate that?
God's Word does.
Exodus 26:7 explains that curtains of goat hair were to be made for the tent over the tabernacle.
Eleven curtains were prescribed for that covering.
The women's work in Exodus 35 contributed to the materials required for the sanctuary.
Their labor was not decorative sentiment.
It served a real purpose in the construction God commanded.
The goat-hair covering was not the innermost curtain of the tabernacle, and Scripture does not say that these women alone constructed the entire covering.
But their contribution was part of the larger work.
That distinction matters.
Because we do not need to exaggerate the biblical account to discover its beauty.
The truth is already powerful enough.
God's work involved different people bringing different gifts, each contributing according to what they had and what they were equipped to do.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to confront our modern obsession with visibility.
We live in a world that measures importance through attention.
How many people watched?
How many applauded?
How many followers did you gain?
How many people know your name?
Even Christian service can become tangled in the desire to be recognized.
We may begin by wanting to glorify God and slowly find ourselves craving the glory that belongs to Him.
But these women leave us with a different picture.
The Bible records their work without preserving their individual names.
Their contribution mattered even though the account does not turn them into celebrities.
And that should make us examine what we really want.
Would you still serve Jesus if nobody publicly thanked you?
Would you still give if nobody knew how much you sacrificed?
Would you still pray for someone who never discovered you were praying?
Would you still do the right thing if your obedience brought no applause?
Those questions are uncomfortable.
They are uncomfortable for me to write, too.
Because it is possible to love the idea of serving God while secretly loving the recognition that sometimes comes with serving Him.
Jesus addressed this danger directly.
In Matthew 6:1, He warned against practicing righteousness before others for the purpose of being seen by them.
He was not forbidding every visible good work. Matthew 5:16 calls believers to let their light shine so that others may glorify the Father.
The difference is the direction of the glory.
Are we trying to make ourselves look important?
Or are we helping others see the goodness of God?
And here is the part that might hurt a little.
Some of us have stopped serving because we felt overlooked.
We gave.
We worked.
We showed up.
We stayed faithful.
Then someone else received the recognition.
Someone else was celebrated.
Someone else got the opportunity.
And something inside us began to grow cold.
We told ourselves we were simply tired.
Sometimes that was true.
But sometimes beneath the exhaustion was an unspoken disappointment:
I thought somebody would notice.
If that describes you, hear this with tenderness.
Being overlooked can genuinely hurt.
Unfair treatment is real.
And faithful service does not mean allowing others to exploit you or refusing necessary rest.
Even Jesus withdrew to pray and rest.
But don't allow another person's failure to appreciate you to become the final measure of your worth before God.
Your identity is not established by how visible your service becomes.
For those who belong to Christ, identity rests in Him.
Colossians 3:23–24 calls believers to work heartily for the Lord, knowing that they serve the Lord Christ.
And the women spinning goat hair remind us that ordinary labor can belong to an extraordinary purpose.
But there is another detail we cannot afford to miss.
The people were not forced into a fundraising competition.
Exodus 35 repeatedly emphasizes willing hearts.
The contributions came from those whose hearts moved them.
Exodus 35:29 describes the offerings as freewill offerings to the Lord.
And later, something remarkable happened.
The people brought so much that the craftsmen reported there was more than enough for the work.
Moses actually commanded the people to stop bringing contributions.
Read Exodus 36:4–7.
Imagine that.
A community giving so willingly and abundantly that its leaders could say, in effect, We have enough. You do not need to bring more.
That is a profound picture of generosity.
But it is also a warning against manipulating people in God's name.
The tabernacle was built through willing contributions, not spiritual intimidation.
And the New Testament carries that principle forward.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
The Greek expression μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης (mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs) communicates that giving should not come from grief or compulsion.
That matters enormously.
Because giving to Christian ministry can be a beautiful expression of worship, gratitude, generosity, and partnership in the Gospel.
No monthly payment makes a person more loved by God.
Your first allegiance belongs to Christ.
Your responsibilities to your household matter.
Your generosity toward your local church, the poor, and those in need matters.
And when you freely choose to support trustworthy ministries that faithfully teach Scripture and serve others, that too can become a meaningful part of your Christian stewardship.
This is why I want to speak to you personally about Gospel Warrior.
If these messages have helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront sin, find encouragement, or remember the mercy of Jesus, then you already understand why this work matters.
Behind every article is a desire that someone, somewhere, might open God's Word instead of surrendering to despair.
That someone struggling with guilt might encounter the message of forgiveness.
That someone spiritually exhausted might be reminded that Christ receives those who come to Him.
That someone who has drifted far from the faith might begin asking serious questions about repentance and restoration.
That someone who has never understood the Gospel might finally hear that salvation is found in Jesus Christ.
And just as the sanctuary involved people contributing different skills and materials, the work of sharing biblical teaching today also involves people giving what they can.
Some write.
Some teach.
Some pray.
Some encourage.
Some share resources.
Some support the practical expenses that make the work possible.
Not everyone can contribute financially.
And no one should feel ashamed of that.
What matters is that your giving is voluntary, thoughtful, and directed toward work you believe is faithful to the Gospel.
It is a practical partnership that can help make continued ministry possible.
These are simply tangible expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards and certainly not substitutes for the riches believers already possess in Christ.
The purpose is simple: to help people become more deeply rooted in Scripture, more discerning in their faith, and more devoted to Jesus Christ.
Because we don't want people merely to feel inspired for five minutes.
We want them to know the Savior.
We want them to read the Bible.
We want them to grow in truth.
We want them to recognize false teaching, resist temptation, pursue holiness, and learn to walk faithfully with Christ when nobody is watching.
And if financial support is not possible, there is still something deeply meaningful you can do.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to make yourself appear religious.
But because somewhere among your friends and family may be a person who believes their ordinary life has no purpose.
Someone who thinks God cannot use them because their past is too damaged.
Someone who has been serving quietly and is close to giving up.
Someone who has confused being unseen by people with being forgotten by God.
You may never know what happens after they read it.
But you can help put the truth in front of them.
Someone who has served without asking for attention.
Someone whose hands have worked tirelessly for others.
Someone who needs to hear that their worth is not measured by public recognition.
And if this story has exposed something personal in you, don't rush past it.
Maybe you've been hiding behind the excuse that you have nothing valuable to offer.
Maybe you've been waiting for a bigger platform before obeying God in smaller things.
Maybe you've been so ashamed of your past that you've forgotten the transforming power of Christ.
Or maybe you've been working so hard for the approval of people that you've lost the joy of serving Jesus.
Be honest before the Lord.
Not as a ritual.
Not as a promise that writing those words will cause a miracle.
But as a simple expression of willingness to place your abilities, opportunities, and everyday responsibilities before Christ.
If God has been teaching you to serve without applause, share a little of that testimony.
Your words may encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
Because the story is not finished.
There is something even more beautiful waiting beyond the wilderness sanctuary.
Centuries after the women of Israel spun goat hair for the tabernacle, the apostle John wrote words that changed the way Christians understand God's dwelling among humanity.
John 1:14 says:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.”
The Greek word translated “dwelt” is ἐσκήνωσεν (eskēnōsen), from a verb associated with pitching a tent or dwelling.
John's language powerfully recalls the biblical theme of God's dwelling among His people.
The tabernacle was not the final destination of that story.
It anticipated something greater.
Not another tent made with human hands.
Not another curtain.
Not another priest whose ministry would end in death.
But Jesus Christ.
The eternal Word made flesh.
The Son of God dwelling among us.
The One who lived without sin.
The One who touched the unclean.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who confronted religious hypocrisy.
The One who willingly went to the cross.
The One who bore our sins and rose again.
And here is the Gospel truth that transforms everything.
The women helped prepare a sanctuary where God's presence would be manifested. Jesus Christ came as the ultimate revelation of God's presence and the perfect mediator who brings sinners near to God.
We do not come to the Father because our work is impressive enough.
We do not enter His presence because our giving is generous enough.
We do not receive eternal life because we have accumulated enough acts of service.
We come through Jesus Christ.
Through His death and resurrection.
Through the grace of God received by faith.
Hebrews 10:19–22 calls believers to draw near with confidence through the blood of Jesus.
And that means the deepest message of this story is not simply that God can use your hands.
It is that Jesus can redeem your life.
Your hands may have done things you regret.
Your heart may have loved things it should have rejected.
Your history may contain choices you wish you could undo.
But repentance and faith in Christ open the way to forgiveness and new life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That does not mean every consequence of sin disappears.
It does not mean every wound heals overnight.
It does not mean the Christian life becomes easy.
But it means your past does not have the authority to define your future apart from the grace of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is the part of the story you needed most.
Because somewhere along the way, you began to believe that your life was too ordinary to matter.
Too damaged to be restored.
Too small to contribute.
Too late to begin again.
But look at the women in Exodus.
They did not need their names engraved on the sanctuary.
They did not need to be the center of the story.
They simply responded with willing hearts and skillful hands.
And their work became part of the place God had commanded His people to prepare.
What if you stopped asking whether your contribution was impressive and started asking whether it was faithful?
What if you stopped comparing your calling with somebody else's?
What if you brought your abilities to Christ without demanding that He make you famous?
What if the next act of obedience He is calling you to is not something spectacular?
Maybe it's making the apology you've delayed.
Maybe it's opening the Bible you've neglected.
Maybe it's confessing the sin you've hidden.
Maybe it's forgiving someone while still maintaining wise boundaries.
Maybe it's returning to a church community where you can grow under sound biblical teaching.
Maybe it's helping someone in need.
Maybe it's faithfully doing the work already entrusted to you.
Or maybe it's using your voice, resources, or online presence to help another person encounter the Gospel.
Whatever it is, remember this:
The value of obedience is not determined by how many people applaud it.
And the beauty of Christian service is not found in making ourselves indispensable.
It is found in belonging to the Savior who alone is sufficient.
The tabernacle was eventually completed.
Exodus 40 records that the glory of the Lord filled it.
The glory belonged to God.
Not to the gold.
Not to the curtains.
Not to the craftsmen.
Not to the women who spun the goat hair.
Their work had served its purpose within God's command.
And all attention ultimately belonged to Him.
That is the kind of life worth living.
Not a life spent trying to convince the world that we are extraordinary.
But a life so surrendered to Jesus that even ordinary things become opportunities to honor Him.
Pray over it.
Return to the Scriptures.
Every prayer matters.
Every faithful act of service matters.
Every opportunity to communicate the Gospel is worth taking seriously.
Not because we can save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because we have been entrusted with the privilege of bearing witness to Him.
And if you are reading this while carrying shame, exhaustion, or the quiet fear that God has forgotten you, I want you to remember the women in the wilderness.
The Bible did not preserve their individual names.
But it preserved the record of their faithfulness.
More importantly, remember the Savior to whom the whole story ultimately points.
The One who knows His sheep.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who makes all things new.
You do not have to build a sanctuary to earn His presence.
You are invited to come to Him through faith.
And when His grace changes your heart, even the ordinary work of your hands can become an expression of love for the One who redeemed you.
The world may never remember what your hands have done, but the greater miracle is that Jesus can redeem the heart behind them.
